raffia.origin: Raffia comes from palms of the genus Raphia (Arecaceae, subfamily Calamoideae), which contains about 22 species centered on tropical Africa, including Raphia vinifera of West and Central Africa; Madagascar also has a long raffia tradition. Some species form large single-species stands in swamps. Raphia vinifera was also introduced long ago to the Brazilian Amazon, where its fiber is now studied for composites. The palms are multipurpose: petioles and leaflets go into buildings, and sap is tapped for palm wine.
raffia.structure: Textile raffia is not a spun staple fiber but a ribbon: the thin epidermal membrane stripped from young leaflets. It is a cellulosic, lignified tissue whose strips can be split to widths suited to weaving or knotting. Stem or petiole fibers, used in composites, are different: bundles that are highly porous and absorbent, with Cameroonian Raphia vinifera stem fibers gaining about 300 to 660 percent of their dry mass in water at saturation. Absorption varies from the periphery to the center of the stem.
raffia.process: The epidermis of young leaflets is peeled away from the underlying tissue in long strips, which are dried and split or trimmed to the width required. Rather than being spun like staple fiber, the strips are used directly: woven as warp and weft on looms, plaited, knotted or crocheted into hats, bags and mats. Finishing and decoration vary by tradition and can include dyeing and embroidery. For composites, raffia fabric or chopped stem fibers are embedded in resins; in one polyester study, alkali treatment lowered composite strength because it weakened fiber to matrix adhesion.
raffia.performance: Raffia strips are flexible and lightweight with useful strength along their length, which suits weaving and plaiting without spinning. As a cellulosic tissue it is hydrophilic, and highly porous raffia stem fibers absorb very large amounts of water, which complicates composite processing. It can be dyed like other cellulosics. Randomly dispersed raffia fibers stiffened a polyester resin, raising its Young's modulus. In epoxy composites tested for ballistic layers, energy absorption fell as raffia fabric content rose from 10 to 30 percent.
raffia.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: natural raffia burns and chars like paper, while plastic raffia ribbon (usually polypropylene) melts and drips and floats on water. Under magnification, natural raffia appears as a thin sheet of plant tissue rather than as separate fibers. FTIR easily separates cellulose from polyolefin. Paper ribbon sold as raffia is another possible substitute and weakens quickly when wetted and rubbed.
raffia.labeling: Raffia palm fiber has no Annex I name in Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011, so EU fibre-composition labels would generally declare it as other fibres with its percentage. In the US, covered textile products must disclose fiber content under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and 16 CFR Part 303; a synthetic ribbon called raffia must carry its generic name, such as polypropylene (an olefin under 16 CFR 303.7). Hats and bags may fall under other product rules, so documentation of fiber identity is advisable.
raffia.past: Raffia cloth is part of long-standing African textile traditions. In the Republic of the Congo, the epidermis of young raffia leaflets is still used to make loincloths and traditional dance skirts, showing that raffia cloth remains in living use. The same palms supply building materials, palm wine and edible larvae, so raffia cloth sits within a wider palm economy. Malagasy raffia weaving and basketry are also long-standing crafts. Global commerce later adopted raffia for hats and garden ties, and the name was borrowed for polypropylene ribbon used in horticulture, which is a different material.

paper-yarn.origin: Paper yarn is made from paper, not from a single plant. The classic Japanese source is washi made from long bast fibers of kozo (paper mulberry, largely the hybrid Broussonetia x kazinoki), mitsumata (Edgeworthia) or gampi (Wikstroemia). Many modern paper yarns are made from wood-pulp papers, for example yarn developed from Swedish forest resources, and research groups have even made yarns from fungal chitin-glucan sheets. Composition therefore depends entirely on the sheet used.
paper-yarn.structure: A paper yarn is a twisted or rolled strip of a nonwoven cellulose network: fibers are held together by hydrogen bonding rather than by twist between staple fibers. Rolling or twisting the strip turns it into a roughly round or oval cross-section, and published paper yarns span about 200 to 1,600 microns in diameter. Long bast fibers in washi give stronger, more flexible sheets than short wood fibers. Because the precursor is an engineered sheet, paper yarns show less biological variability than natural staple fibers, but their properties track sheet grammage and fiber quality.
paper-yarn.process: In shifu, the Japanese handcraft, washi is cut with a sharp knife or blade into strips about 1 to 3 mm wide. The strips are crumpled and slightly moistened to reduce stiffness, then rolled between the fingers or over a rough surface to round them, and spun and twisted while still damp; new strips are added by overlapping their ends and twisting them together, forming a continuous yarn. The yarn is dried and woven. Industrial paper yarn follows the same logic at scale: paper is cut into narrow tapes and twisted, and finishing agents are applied to improve knittability and washing stability.
paper-yarn.performance: Paper yarns have tenacity broadly similar to cotton yarns, reported at about 5 to 17 cN/tex dry, but they weaken markedly when wet as water disrupts fiber-to-fiber hydrogen bonds; one commercial yarn fell from about 7.5 to 4.8 cN/tex. Washing shrinkage is low, about 5 percent or less, compared with about 12 to 15 percent for cotton and 19 to 26 percent for viscose yarns in one comparison. Paper yarn fabrics are light, crisp and breathable. Newer finished paper yarns have retained over 89 percent of breaking strength after 15 washes.
paper-yarn.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: paper yarn burns like any cellulose, fast with paper smell and gray ash. Untwisting a paper yarn reveals a flat strip of matted fibers rather than parallel staple fibers, which is diagnostic. Microscopy of the strip shows a random fiber network typical of paper, and fiber species (kozo, mitsumata, wood pulp) can be judged from cell morphology and staining. Paper yarn is sometimes confused with raffia or with regenerated cellulose ribbons.
paper-yarn.labeling: Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 has no Annex I entry for paper as a fibre name, so the correct declaration for paper yarn, for example naming the constituent cellulose or using other fibres, should be checked with the competent authority or a testing laboratory. In the US, covered textiles must disclose fiber content under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and 16 CFR Part 303. Certification claims for the paper source, such as FSC or PEFC chain of custody, should be backed by certificates from the supplier.
paper-yarn.past: Shifu is an old Japanese craft for turning washi into woven cloth, and it experienced a resurgence in popularity for clothing in the twentieth century. Kozo paper itself rests on Broussonetia, whose role in early Chinese papermaking is traditionally credited to Cai Lun. Paper yarns have recently returned as sustainable fashion materials, including knittable paper yarn developed from Swedish forest resources, wash-stable paper yarns tested for clothing fabrics, and experimental fungal yarns made with shifu techniques.
